reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: A hypertrophied anal papilla is a benign enlargement of one of the normal papillae at the dentate line, projecting from the anal transition zone on a fibrous stalk
It is a common finding in association with chronic anal fissure and chronic inflammation, and is entirely benign with no malignant potential
When enlarged it may be felt as a firm mobile lump, and a longer-stalked papilla can prolapse through the anus during defecation and reduce spontaneously or need manual reduction
Symptoms, when present, include a sensation of a lump, prolapse, pruritus, mucus, mild bleeding, and incomplete evacuation, though many are asymptomatic
It is frequently confused clinically with an internal haemorrhoid or a rectal polyp, but its origin at the dentate line and pale fibrous appearance help distinguish it
Because it arises at the dentate line it is covered by sensate anoderm-transitional epithelium, so instrumentation without anaesthesia can be painful
Management is reassurance for asymptomatic lesions and simple excision for symptomatic or prolapsing papillae, ideally with any coexisting fissure treated
Excised or atypical lesions should undergo histology to confirm the benign fibroepithelial nature and exclude a neoplastic polyp
reference.pathophysiology: The anal papillae are small triangular projections situated at the dentate line at the free edges of the anal valves, representing normal remnants of the embryological anal membrane. Chronic irritation and inflammation, most typically from a chronic anal fissure but also from recurrent low-grade infection or inflammatory conditions, provoke reactive fibrous hypertrophy of a papilla. The papilla enlarges into a firm, pale, fibroepithelial polypoid structure covered by squamous or transitional epithelium. With a sufficiently long stalk it may prolapse through the anal canal during straining. The lesion is composed of fibrovascular connective tissue and is entirely benign, but its enlargement produces local symptoms and can mimic other anal lumps.
additionalDifferentials: Anal skin tag or fibroepithelial anal polyp of the margin
Anal intraepithelial neoplasia or anal carcinoma
Sentinel tag of a chronic anal fissure
Hypertrophic mucosal fold of rectal prolapse
additionalInvestigations: Inspection and digital rectal examination to localise the lesion to the dentate line
Proctoscopy or anoscopy to visualise the papilla and any coexisting fissure or haemorrhoids
Examination under anaesthesia where pain limits assessment or a fissure is present
Histopathology of any excised or atypical lesion to confirm benign fibroepithelial tissue
Colonoscopy where a proximal polyp or neoplasm needs exclusion in symptomatic bleeding
Assessment for an underlying chronic fissure as the driving cause
redFlags: Induration, ulceration, or irregular surface suggesting neoplasia
Rapid growth or change in a previously stable lump
Bleeding out of keeping with a benign papilla
A lesion arising above the dentate line, prompting exclusion of a rectal polyp or tumour
Associated non-healing fissure or perianal Crohn features
reference.prognosis: A hypertrophied anal papilla is benign with an excellent prognosis; it carries no malignant potential and, when symptomatic, is cured by simple excision, though it may recur if an underlying chronic fissure or ongoing irritation is not addressed.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for a haemorrhoid and treating accordingly, leaving the papilla and fissure unaddressed
Instrumenting or banding a sensate dentate-line lesion without anaesthesia, causing severe pain
Failing to send excised tissue for histology and missing a neoplastic polyp
Overlooking and not treating the coexisting chronic fissure driving the hypertrophy
Offering surgery for an incidental asymptomatic papilla

Standard coloproctology reference texts on benign anal lesions
Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland guidance on benign anorectal conditions
management: Reassurance about the benign, non-malignant nature where the papilla is small or asymptomatic
Treat the underlying chronic anal fissure or ongoing anal irritation to remove the driving stimulus
Optimise stool consistency and bowel habit with fibre, fluids and stool softeners to reduce straining and prolapse
Surgical excision of a symptomatic, prolapsing or persistently troublesome papilla, which is curative
Perform examination or excision under anaesthesia given the sensate transitional epithelium at the dentate line
Histological confirmation of excised or atypical lesions, with proctoscopy or colonoscopy to exclude other anorectal pathology
